hook.line: Lucía from Madrid says *hoy he desayunado* where you would say *hoy desayuné*. Same meaning, different habit, and it will be in every conversation with someone from Spain.
hook.en: I had breakfast at home today.

examples.en: I had breakfast at home today.

examples.es: Esta mañana he ido al médico.
examples.en: I went to the doctor this morning.
Have you seen Vale today? (to a friend)

examples.es: Esta tarde han llamado de la oficina.

examples.en: I went to the market yesterday.

rule:
In Colombia, anything finished goes in the simple past: *Hoy desayuné.* *Esta mañana fui al médico.*

In Spain, if the time is still going (*hoy*, *esta mañana*, *esta semana*, *este año*), they use *he* + participle: *Hoy he desayunado.* *Esta mañana he ido al médico.*

So the *he* form does not mean *I have* here. It is just a past, and your English *I had breakfast* is the right idea.

Once the time is over, both countries agree: *Ayer fui al mercado.*

You do not need to produce this. Understand it, and know that it is a normal accent, not a mistake. Keep the *he* form for experience and for "not yet", as in *¿Has estado en Cartagena?* and *Todavía no he terminado.* One more Spain habit: *esta noche* can mean last night, so *Esta noche he dormido fatal* is about the night that just ended.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the *pretérito perfecto compuesto*. In Spain it covers a past that still touches the present.

readAndPick.es: Esta mañana he ido al médico.
options: I'm going to the doctor this morning.
I went to the doctor this morning.
I used to go to the doctor in the mornings.
Do you see Vale every day?

readAndPick.es: Esta tarde han llamado de la oficina.
options: The office will call this afternoon.
I will travel a lot this year.
I traveled a lot last year.
I have traveled a lot this year.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *he ido* or *fui* and type the whole sentence, the way Lucía says it: *Esta mañana ___ al médico.*
yourTurn.answer: Esta mañana he ido al médico.
yourTurn.why: Lucía's morning is still today, so Spain uses *he* + the participle *ido*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *hemos abierto* or *abrimos* and type the whole sentence, the way it's said in Colombia: *Hoy ___ tarde.*
yourTurn.why: In Colombia a finished event stays in the simple past, even for today.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it like Lucía: I had breakfast at home today.
yourTurn.why: *Hoy* is still going, so Spain says *he desayunado*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it like Lucía, to a friend: Have you eaten today?
yourTurn.why: *Has* is the helper for *tú*, and the participle *comido* never changes.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it the Colombian way: *Hoy he llegado temprano.*
yourTurn.why: Colombia swaps *he llegado* for the simple past *llegué*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it the Spain way: *Hoy hablé con Vale.*
yourTurn.why: Spain uses *he* + participle for today: *he hablado*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Hoy he tomado café.*

pitfalls.why: Even in Spain, *ayer* is over, so it takes the simple past. The *he* form is for time that is still today.

pitfalls.wrong: Esta mañana he fui al médico.
pitfalls.right: Esta mañana he ido al médico.
pitfalls.why: After *he* you need the participle *ido*, not the simple past.
The participle ends in *-ado* or *-ido* and never changes. The person lives in *he*.

personal: Tell Lucía one thing you have done today, the Madrid way, starting with *Hoy he…* or *Esta mañana he…*, for example *Hoy he trabajado mucho.*
